lead.headline: The Pacific Heads for the Strongest El Niño Ever Measured
lead.deck: Forecasters expect the central Pacific to run 3.7°C above normal this autumn, far beyond the 2015 record. Its effects will reach almost every continent.
body: Normally, trade winds push warm surface water west across the tropical Pacific, so it piles up near Indonesia and Australia while cooler water wells up off South America. Every few years the winds slacken, the warm pool sloshes east, and the atmosphere above it reorganises. That is El Niño.

This year's event is off the charts. The World Meteorological Organization forecasts that the key index, the temperature anomaly in a box of the central Pacific called Niño 3.4, will average about +3.7°C from October to December. That would be the highest since observations began, well above the previous record of +2.6°C in late 2015. The anomaly has climbed fast: about +1.6°C in June, +2.5°C in August.

Daily readings have already passed the 2015 peak. The Boston Globe reported values above 3.4°C over normal, against a 2015 peak of 3.08°C, and the Washington Post projects that the event could peak near 4.2°C in December.

The US Climate Prediction Center, in its October 8 update, gave an 83% chance that the coming months will produce an event stronger than any since 1950. The WMO puts the chance it lasts through February at close to 100%. Figures differ by index: NOAA uses a relative measure that strips out the ocean's long-term warming, so its numbers run lower.

The event arrives on top of an already warmer world. Ahead of COP31, the UN pointed to this year's record-breaking heat, devastating floods and an "unprecedented" El Niño as reasons to speed up climate action.

map.title: THE TROPICAL PACIFIC
map.footnote: Warm water shifts east when trade winds weaken
map.caption: El Niño moves the Pacific's warm pool from Asia toward the Americas.

lead.why: El Niño shifts rainfall around the planet: historically it has brought drought to Australia, Indonesia and southern Africa, floods to Peru and the southern United States, and a temporary jump in global average temperature on top of long-term warming. A record event arriving as countries prepare for the COP31 climate summit will test how much damage early warnings can prevent.

world.headline: Ebola Crosses Into Kenya as an Outbreak With No Vaccine Grows
world.deck: A traveller from Congo died in Nairobi of the Bundibugyo strain. More than 8,700 people have been confirmed infected since the outbreak began.
body: On October 6 Kenya confirmed its first case in the current Ebola outbreak. The patient, a Kenyan who fell ill while living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, travelled through Uganda and flew to Nairobi on October 3. The patient was isolated on arrival and died on October 5. Health officials are tracing 28 contacts, including 23 passengers and four crew from his flight.

The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, one of several viruses that cause Ebola disease. As of October 6 the World Health Organization counted 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths, mostly in Congo's Ituri and North Kivu provinces. Kenya is the fourth country to report a case. WHO declared the outbreak a global health emergency in May.

Kenyan officials stress that the country does not have an outbreak: this is a single imported case, and response teams in Kenya and Uganda have begun tracing everyone the patient met. In Congo, Ituri province alone has recorded about 6,450 cases across 28 of its 36 health zones, according to one report. With the virus killing about half of those confirmed infected, every missed contact matters.
Unlike the more familiar Zaire strain, Bundibugyo has no approved vaccine or specific treatment, so care relies on fluids, oxygen and treating symptoms.
The World Health Organization is supporting Kenya's response, and IGAD, the East African regional bloc, has stepped up preparedness among its member states.

chart.title: THE OUTBREAK SO FAR
chart.subtitle: Confirmed, as of October 6
chart.caption: About 48% of confirmed cases have died, according to WHO.

world.connect: Ebola viruses live in wild animals, most likely fruit bats, and spill into people through contact with infected animals or their blood. The Bundibugyo strain is named after the district in western Uganda where it was first identified in 2007. Outbreaks are often worst where clinics are few and conflict makes contact tracing dangerous, which describes much of eastern Congo. The largest Ebola epidemic on record, in West Africa in 2014-16, was caused by the Zaire strain, for which vaccines now exist.

climate_and_environment.headline: In Tuvalu, Leaders Start Admitting 1.5°C Will Be Overshot
climate_and_environment.deck: A pre-summit meeting in the Pacific set the stage for November's COP31 in Turkey, where Australia will lead the negotiations.
body: Australia co-hosted this week's Pacific "pre-COP" with Fiji and Tuvalu: officials met in Nadi, Fiji, from October 5 to 8, and leaders spent a day in Tuvalu, a nation of low coral islands that rising seas threaten. It was Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's first official visit there. In Tuvalu, he said, climate change is not a problem for the future. Only two leaders from outside the Pacific accepted Australia's invitation, and Albanese warned Australians to expect an extreme-weather summer.

The meeting prepares COP31, the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20. Turkey hosts it, while Australia presides over the negotiations. The summit's president, Murat Kurum, called the 1.5°C warming limit "a matter of survival" for the Pacific.

Yet Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, said the summit's main decision could acknowledge that overshooting 1.5°C is now inevitable. The UN's message ahead of the summit was that "overshoot is not a reason to surrender": every fraction of a degree avoided still matters.
The scale of the gap is the theme the Pacific hosts pressed hardest: leaders were urged to close the distance between what countries have promised and what they have actually delivered.
climate_and_environment.why: The 1.5°C goal in the Paris Agreement has framed climate diplomacy for a decade. Admitting it will be exceeded shifts the debate to how far and for how long, and to who pays for adapting to the damage.

science_and_technology.kicker: SCIENCE & TECH  •  NOBEL PRIZE IN CHEMISTRY
science_and_technology.headline: Why Life Is Left-Handed: Chemistry Nobel for Mirror-Image Molecules
science_and_technology.deck: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai showed how reactions can favour one 'hand' of a molecule, and even amplify it.
body: Many molecules come in two versions that are mirror images, like your left and right hands: same atoms, same connections, but they cannot be stacked on top of each other. Chemists call this chirality. Living things are strikingly one-handed, building proteins from almost only left-handed amino acids.

On October 7 the Nobel committee honoured Henri Kagan of Université Paris-Saclay and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis". Kagan showed that a slightly lopsided catalyst can produce a much more lopsided product. Soai found a reaction whose product speeds up its own formation, amplifying a tiny excess of one hand into near-purity.

Soai's reaction matters beyond the lab because it shows how a tiny, random imbalance could snowball. On the early Earth, a chance excess of one hand might have been amplified the same way until life's chemistry was almost entirely one-handed. Each Nobel this year is worth 12 million Swedish crowns, about $1.2 million, shared between the winners.
science_and_technology.why: The wrong hand can be dangerous: thalidomide, given to pregnant women in the 1950s and 60s as a mixture of both hands, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies. Today regulators expect drug makers to study each hand separately. Kagan and Soai's work helps chemists make single-hand molecules and offers a clue to how early life came to favour one hand.

did_you_know.text: El Niño, Spanish for 'the boy', was named by fishermen in Peru, who noticed that a warm current sometimes arrived off their coast around Christmas and emptied their nets. The name refers to the infant Jesus. Its cold opposite is called La Niña, 'the girl'.

explainer.title: How the Pacific sets the world's weather
body: The tropical Pacific is the largest stretch of warm ocean on Earth, and warm water feeds the air above it with heat and moisture. Where the warmest water sits, air rises and storms form; where it is cooler, air sinks and skies stay dry. Normally that pattern puts heavy rain over Indonesia and dry air off Peru.

When El Niño shifts the warm water east, the rain belt follows it. That moves the jet streams, the high rivers of wind that steer weather systems, so the effects travel thousands of kilometres. It also changes the winds high above the Atlantic, which tends to tear apart growing storms there and is one reason El Niño years usually see fewer Atlantic hurricanes.

Scientists track all this with a line of buoys moored across the equatorial Pacific, which measure water temperature from the surface down hundreds of metres, and with satellites that measure sea-surface height: warm water expands, so the sea literally rises where El Niño's heat collects.
Because the ocean releases extra heat into the air, the year after a strong El Niño is often among the warmest on record globally.

Strong El Niños usually peak around December and fade by late spring. They are often followed by La Niña, the cool opposite phase, which pushes the warm water back west and flips many of the same weather effects.
